## What We Did

1.  The lab question: a housing agency wants an *expected* rent for
    every Philadelphia tract. This is a ŷ (y-hat) problem, not a β̂
    (beta-hat) problem. ŷ = prediction: guess a number for each row. β̂ =
    inference: ask why / does X cause Y?

2.  get_acs(... , geometry = TRUE) with more variables: med_rent =
    "B25064_001" \# median gross rent (our Y) med_inc = "B19013_001" \#
    median household income renter_occ, occ_units, education variables
    (ba, ma, prof, phd)

3.  Build variables with mutate(): pct_renter = renter_occE / occ_unitsE
    \* 100 pct_ba = (baE + maE + profE + phdE) / total_popE \* 100
    rent_se = med_rentM / 1.645 \# standard error from margin of error
    rent_cv = rent_se / med_rentE \* 100 \# coefficient of variation:
    how noisy is one estimate?

4.  Count Indego stations within half a mile of each tract (Week 4
    tools): st_is_within_distance(tracts, stations, dist = 0.5) \#
    returns a list, one element per tract lengths(...) \# turns the list
    into a plain numeric vector: n_stations

5.  Drop rows with missing Y or X yourself, on purpose:
    filter(total_popE \> 0, !is.na(med_rentE), !is.na(med_incE), ...) \#
    R drops them quietly otherwise, and then residuals won't line up
    with tracts.

6.  Plot before modeling: ggplot(tracts, aes(x = med_incE, y =
    med_rentE)) + geom_point() + geom_smooth(method = "lm") \# "Fits"
    means dots sit close to a straight line, NOT that rent equals income
    in value.

7.  Fit m1: lm(med_rentE \~ med_incE) rent = intercept + coefficient ×
    income + residual coef ≈ 0.008 → +\$10,000 income predicts about
    +\$80 rent per month. Small effect. Tiny p-value does NOT mean the
    effect is big. p-value is about β̂ (is it real?).

8.  Fit m2: lm(med_rentE \~ med_incE + pct_renter + pct_ba + n_stations)
    Read one coefficient two ways:

    -   β̂ reading: bike stations don't "raise" rents; the coefficient
        soaks up neighborhood character (multicollinearity), so no
        causal claim.
    -   ŷ reading: keep the variable if it helps guess rent on new
        tracts.

9.  Check survey noise: plot abs(residual) vs rent_cv. Big miss + high
    CV = maybe survey noise, not model failure. Don't trust those
    tracts.

10. Train/test split (80/20), then 10-fold cross-validation with caret:
    trainControl(method = "cv", number = 10); train(..., method = "lm",
    trControl = ctrl) \# set.seed(5080) before each train() so every
    model gets the same folds: fair comparison. \# The grade is CV RMSE:
    average miss in dollars on data the model never saw. Lower = better.
    \# R² always rises when you add variables, so it can never tell you
    the new variables truly help.

11. Where is the model wrong? Residuals vs fitted + bptest(m2); map
    residuals with geom_sf(). Red = rent higher than predicted. Errors
    cluster (University City, Northeast): the model is missing something
    about those places.

12. Challenge: build the best rent prediction model. Lowest CV RMSE
    wins. Rule: no leakage — cannot use anything built from rent itself
    (med_rentM, rent_cv, rent burden...). Deliver: CV RMSE in dollars,
    one new feature + why, one coefficient read twice, top-5 tracts with
    rent far above prediction (with rent CV: trust or fog?), residual
    map.

## Key Concepts

This lab was an introduction to machine learning for prediction, using
linear regression. The core distinction is prediction (ŷ) versus
inference (β̂): prediction asks "what will Y be for a new row," while
inference asks "does X cause Y and by how much." The same coefficient
gets read two different ways depending on the task. For grading a
prediction model we use out-of-sample error: split the data into train
and test sets, or better, use k-fold cross-validation, and report RMSE —
the typical miss in dollars on unseen data. In-sample R² always improves
when variables are added, so it cannot judge whether new variables truly
help; CV RMSE can get worse, which makes it the honest grade. I also
learned that our Y itself is noisy: ACS rent estimates carry margins of
error, and a large residual in a high-CV tract may be survey fog rather
than signal. Finally, mapping residuals showed that errors are not
random in space — they cluster — which means the model is missing real
spatial structure.

## Reflection

This lab changed how I read regression output. Before, I thought a
significant p-value meant a variable was "good." Now I see the p-value
answers the inference question, while prediction is graded by CV RMSE on
data the model has never seen — and a variable can fail the first test
but pass the second. Plotting the residuals on a map was the most
surprising part: the red clusters made it obvious that the model doesn't
know something about University City and the Northeast, and no table of
coefficients shows that as clearly. The hardest part is letting go of
causal language: it feels natural to say "stations raise rents," but for
this task all that matters is whether the variable helps the guess.

## Questions I Still Have

If CV RMSE is the only grade for prediction, when would I ever care
about R² again? And how do I decide how much survey noise is "too much"
before I stop trusting a tract's residual?
